title: Some Articles I Didn't Finish in 2024
subtitle: A year in incomplete writing
text:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is quixotic. I try—valiantly— to generate a new article (or video or podcast) daily. Today, we review the articles that weren’t. The articles you didn't read, in case I couldn’t get them done for one reason or another. It’s a “behind the scenes” year in review of my…the lowlights of my myriad failures to bring you content that, absent this article, you'd remain blissfully unaware of. Fear not! My failure laid out transparently, is what today’s article is about.

Medical Boards Won't Save Us

Here is a video setting up some incredible prose that never became a Real Article.

I want to think that having licensed professionals means that there is oversight of those individuals. I want to believe that when I see a doctor, I will be safe. You probably want the same thing. The process of medical licensure is extremely elaborate. It involves fingerprinting. It involves criminal background checks. It involves sending in certified copies of examination reports; it is a massive pain in the butt, frankly. There is a lot of credentialing by individual employers who also review all this material. It seems like an extensive process; if something went wrong with the behavior of a professional with one of those fancy licenses, such as medicine, psychology, or another profession, the public would be the first to know. We imagine that the investigations will be in-depth.

Whistleblowers would be treated—in our minds— with the utmost respect, and their concerns would be taken very seriously. This is what happens much of the time. This is a deeply personal matter to me because I've had to go through the process—a process I respected—of investigation by the medical board in my state.

Doesn’t it sound like it would have been an excellent article? It gets more spicy from there, but sadly, it isn’t done… and thus won’t happen in the waning hours of 2024.

Owen Muir, M.D. Presents: The 700th Installment of this Newsletter

This article, for those keeping score at home, is number 810. I had an article lined up for my 700th post but blew past it, so obviously, it's not worth finishing. Here are a few gems from that discarded exercise…

This newsletter started with an op-ed I couldn't get anyone to pick up! I learned today that it feeds Google News alerts! I even have a muck-rack. I became…a journalist, not just a hype-man. Although, at the time, writing about the impact of Supreme Court decisions on ERISA seemed pretty niche, litigation has picked up quite a bit in the subsequent two years.

This newsletter has picked up a lot since the beginning. It has racked up over 1.5 million views from more than 600,000 persons who read this publication. As of today, I have 200 paid subscribers.

Quite the victory lap. I know. I also thank my contributors, which I will do here as well:

I edit and write this newsletter to entertain my readers, and I enjoy it. It has, however, taken on a life of its own. Initially, it was an attempt to take control of a narrative I didn't feel communicated what I thought was important. I wanted to focus on justice for patients, equitable access to care, and better outcomes in human health. I think we’ve done that. Like any real accomplishment, The Frontier Psychiatrists has grown beyond just one person. It has become a place where other writers can express their opinions about what should be better. I've been honored to share this corner of the Internet with friends, colleagues, and even those with dissenting views. Writers like:

and many more.

I feel mild to moderately bad that I didn’t get to thank them in that article, so I have shoe horned it in here.

My Pants Are Not On Fire

I have zero idea what this article was going to be about. I have just that amazing title, and the following text:

The Frontier psychiatrists is a health themed newsletter that does some interesting legal hate-watching of big health care congressional testimony.

As I reported recently,

Maybe I was going to write about the PBM CEOs getting grilled? But I did that in this podcast here. I have no idea. It’s such a funny title, but the intent was lost to time.

Building Nothing Out of Something

This is another amazing title that ended up not being an article. I think I was going to make fun of Talkiatry, the telehealth company that hires a lot of good psychiatrists and then prevents them from taking high acuity cases. This wastes crucial resources. Alas, I never even got started on the article. We are bereft of whatever that presumably scalding critique might have been.

Don’t worry—Talkiatry doesn’t like The Frontier Psychiatrists either. I’m not burning a bridge that existed, here. People talk, Talkiatry. It’s even in your company’s name. They raised $130M in their Series C…and will in theory now do value based something? With glassdoor reviews like this, what could go wrong?

Moving on.

Why Can't I Be Approached to Spread Russian Propaganda Too?

This was a funny enough pretense to get a title out of, but not enough of an orthogonal angle to get an entire article out of.

I write a lot. I write every day. I have opinions. Some of them are distasteful to people. I'm clearly ready to advance an agenda. Is my agenda of advocating for fairness in the payment of healthcare, benefits, and compliance with ERISA too niche for the Russian government? Do other autocrats find my writing impenetrable? I think it's unfair. I'm an influencer, according to me, and yet there is no international psychological operations funding for me! This seems unfair.

This is the MAGIC I need to capture with the newsletter—it’s not enough to have a take. It has to be a HOT take. I need to have some off angle way of thinking about a news item that is unexpected enough to get me through an article in can write, more or less, in one sitting. And this was just too obvious a story—about russia paying for propaganda, to have something interesting to say about it. Propaganda: Bad. Not an article that works in this newsletter.

It is too expected. No article there, not for me.

Even If The Heavens Fall

This was going to be an article about ethics and The Trolley Problem. Again, no orthogonal take to be had:

I’m studying for my maintenance of certification (MOC) as a general and child psychiatrist. This requires us to read articles, now, or take an exam. I’d probably prefer the exam, but I wanted to experience the same thrill reading articles as my colleagues. I’m reading about “The Trolley Problem” today.

So I never finished it. Ethics: it’s always in conflict. Maybe I’ll get an article out of it, but 2024 won’t be that year.

Not All That Is Therapeutic is Therapy: Saving MDMA, Part VI

I got so many article out of the MDMA isn’t getting approved story it’s almost unfair to tell you there was yet anohter I was going to write. Sexual assault shouldn’t happen in clincial trials. Yet, it did:

The Frontier Psychiatrists is making a point about MDMA-assisted therapy, which is that it's a bad idea. And there are better ideas. We're getting to the better ideas in this sixth part of my multi-part series on the topic.

Did you know that alcohol is legal in America? It's true. We have locations in which people regularly ingest this dangerous intoxicant. Some of these are regulated. No physician is available on site. There have been multiple attempts to wipe out these dangerous dens of inequity, but powerful forces, through robust lobbying, even undid a constitutional amendment.

25% of women have experienced sexual assault—including 18% who have been victims of rape.1 Men are not excluded from this, but women are overwhelmingly the more common victims. Similarly, the majority of post-traumatic stress disorder is a consequence of these sexual assaults—only a minority, albeit a crucial cohort to whom we all owe a debt, are male military veterans with combat-related trauma:

At least one-half of all violent crimes involve alcohol consumption by the perpetrator, the victim, or both. Sexual assault fits this pattern. Thus, across the disparate populations studied, researchers consistently have found that approximately one-half of all sexual assaults are committed by men who have been drinking alcohol. Depending on the sample studied and the measures used, the estimates for alcohol use among perpetrators have ranged from 34 to 74 percent. Similarly, approximately one-half of all sexual assault victims report that they were drinking alcohol at the time of the assault, with estimates ranging from 30 to 79 percent.2

And now, the shocking reality: bars are legal. You can go into a bar and buy a drink, and that's completely legal. You can go into a liquor store and buy a bag full of alcoholic drinks, and that's also legal. You can even buy cigarettes at the same time, a leading cause of lung cancer and death. Alcohol is a leading driver of sexual assault—in one remarkable program in Italy focusing on victims of rape, they found the following:

222 patients were enrolled, 25 of which were minors…and most of them knew their aggressor and were raped in a private home. 155 of them …[reported ingesting]…alcoholic substances and/or drugs in conjunction with the event (86 reported having drunk alcohol, 36 having taken drugs and 33 disclosed both alcohol and drug abuse). If the woman knew her abuser, alcohol consumption was described as voluntary in more than 80% of cases, while in relation to drugs the consumption was equally voluntary or fraudulent.3

Again, this alcohol substance? It is legal—there are limited regulations related to the age of the individual purchasing the substance, but it’s without a prescription or medical oversight.

This ended up being a point better made with other data in other articles. So, I moved on.

The Frontier Psychaitrists—they aren’t all gems. That is the story. To more engaging content in 2025!
